items.prompt: What is "black politics" as this unit defines it?
choices: Political tactics that advance someone's position at another person's expense, typically through concealment, deception, or deniability
Any attempt to influence a decision at work, regardless of method
Formal disciplinary action taken by HR against an employee
A negotiation tactic used exclusively in salary discussions
items.explanation: Black politics is specifically defined by concealment/deception at someone else's expense — not by influence-seeking in general, HR action, or salary negotiation.

items.prompt: How does this unit relate "black" politics to the earlier "white" politics unit in this track?
choices: Black politics is presented as the counterpart to white politics — tactics that advance one person's position at another's expense, rather than transparently advancing shared goals
Black politics and white politics are described as identical concepts with different names
Black politics is described as simply a more aggressive version of white politics with no other difference
The unit states white politics no longer applies once black politics tactics are present
items.explanation: L1 explicitly frames black politics as the counterpart to white politics — self-serving and often hidden, versus transparent and shared-goal-advancing.

items.prompt: What is "credit-stealing"?
choices: Presenting someone else's work, analysis, or idea as your own, or allowing others to believe it's yours without correcting them
Asking a colleague for feedback on a shared project
Formally requesting a raise based on recent accomplishments
Publicly thanking a teammate for their contribution to a project
items.explanation: Credit-stealing specifically means claiming or allowing false claim to someone else's work — not feedback requests, raise negotiations, or genuine public credit.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, why is credit-stealing described as "low-risk" for the person doing it?
choices: It's often deniable ("I didn't mean to leave you out") and hard to prove intent behind
Because it's technically legal in every jurisdiction
Because most companies have no policy against it whatsoever
Because it never actually damages the relationship between colleagues
items.explanation: L1 identifies deniability specifically as what makes credit-stealing low-risk — not legality, policy gaps, or an absence of relationship damage.

items.prompt: What is "scapegoating"?
choices: Deliberately directing blame for a shared or someone else's failure onto a person who wasn't actually responsible for it
Publicly acknowledging your own mistake in a project retrospective
Assigning a task to a specific team member based on their skill set
Reviewing a colleague's code and pointing out a genuine bug they introduced
items.explanation: Scapegoating specifically means misdirecting blame onto someone not actually responsible — not honest self-accountability, task assignment, or legitimate code review.

items.prompt: Per L1, does recognizing scapegoating typically require different evidence than recognizing credit-stealing?
choices: Yes — scapegoating usually requires noticing a pattern over time, while credit-stealing is often visible in a single specific moment
No — both require identical evidence in every case
Yes, but only because scapegoating is illegal and credit-stealing is not
No — neither tactic can ever be recognized with any confidence
items.explanation: L2 explicitly distinguishes the evidence needed: credit-stealing often shows up in one clear moment, while scapegoating usually needs a pattern to be visible.

items.prompt: What is "manufactured urgency"?
choices: Falsely framing a request or decision as more time-critical than it actually is, typically to bypass normal scrutiny
A genuinely urgent production incident that requires an immediate response
A project deadline set by a client contract
A calendar reminder set for an upcoming meeting
items.explanation: Manufactured urgency is specifically about falsely inflated time pressure used to avoid scrutiny — not genuine incidents, contractual deadlines, or ordinary reminders.

items.prompt: Why would someone use manufactured urgency as a black-politics tactic?
choices: To push a decision through before objections can form or normal scrutiny can be applied
To give colleagues more time to carefully review a proposal
To comply with a legally mandated deadline
To publicly demonstrate strong project management skills
items.explanation: The tactic's purpose is specifically to compress the window for scrutiny and objection — the opposite of giving more review time or following a legitimate deadline.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, did the colleague plausibly not know whose analysis they were presenting?
choices: No — the Scenario states the colleague knew exactly whose analysis this was
Yes — the Scenario states the colleague genuinely didn't know who built the analysis
It's impossible to tell from the Scenario's facts
The Scenario doesn't address whether the colleague knew or not
items.explanation: The Scenario is explicit that the colleague knew whose work this was — that's part of what distinguishes this from an innocent mix-up.

items.prompt: Per L1, why does it matter to correctly name what happened in the Scenario, rather than just letting it go?
choices: The appropriate response to a genuine misunderstanding differs from the appropriate response to a deliberate pattern, so an accurate read matters for choosing the right response
Naming it correctly guarantees the colleague will be immediately fired
It doesn't actually matter — the response would be identical either way
Naming it correctly is only useful for filing a formal legal complaint
items.explanation: L1 frames accurate recognition as practically useful for calibrating the response — not as an end in itself or a path to punishment.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what does "sabotage" specifically involve?
choices: Deliberately undermining someone else's work or standing, often while appearing supportive
Openly and publicly criticizing a colleague's proposal in a team meeting
Declining to collaborate on a project due to a scheduling conflict
Reporting a genuine ethics violation through official channels
items.explanation: Sabotage specifically involves undermining someone while maintaining an appearance of support — not open criticism, scheduling conflicts, or legitimate reporting.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what defines "weaponized rumors" specifically?
choices: Spreading unverified or false information to damage someone's reputation, with the source hidden
Sharing publicly available, accurate information about a company announcement
Asking a colleague directly whether a rumor you heard is true
Correcting a factual error in a public company memo
items.explanation: Weaponized rumors specifically involve unverified/false claims with a hidden source aimed at reputational damage — not accurate public information or good-faith fact-checking.

items.prompt: Per L2's diagram, what is the actual dividing line between white and black politics?
choices: Whether the tactic is transparent and could survive being stated openly, versus depending on concealment or deception to work
Whether the tactic involves talking to more than one person at a time
Whether the tactic is used by someone in a management role versus an individual contributor
Whether the tactic results in a successful outcome for the person using it
items.explanation: L2 identifies transparency/openness as the actual dividing line — not the number of people involved, seniority, or outcome success.

items.prompt: Per L2, does trying to influence an outcome at work automatically count as black politics?
choices: No — every functioning workplace involves trying to influence outcomes; the dividing line is transparency, not influence-seeking itself
Yes — any attempt to influence a decision is black politics by definition
No, but only for decisions that don't involve money or budget
Yes, but only if more than one person is involved in the attempt
items.explanation: L2 explicitly rejects the idea that influence-seeking itself is the problem — the diagram's dividing question is about transparency, not the presence of influence attempts.

items.prompt: Per L2, why don't more people confront credit-stealing directly when it happens?
choices: The tactic is usually built with deniability in mind, making a direct public accusation risky if the pattern isn't yet established
Because credit-stealing is extremely rare and most people never encounter it
Because company policy universally prohibits ever discussing credit disputes
Because credit-stealing is always immediately obvious and self-evident to everyone present
items.explanation: L2 identifies built-in deniability as the specific reason direct confrontation feels risky — not rarity, policy, or self-evidence.

items.prompt: Per L2, does a single ambiguous incident of possible credit-stealing warrant being ignored entirely?
choices: Not necessarily — but the response to a single incident should usually differ from the response to an established pattern
Yes — a single incident should always be completely ignored regardless of context
No — a single incident should always trigger immediate formal escalation
Yes, because a single incident can never be evidence of anything
items.explanation: L2 calibrates the response by pattern strength rather than recommending either blanket ignoring or blanket escalation for a single incident.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's the risk of treating every uncredited mention as deliberate credit-stealing?
choices: Genuine oversights happen, and jumping to the worst interpretation on a single incident can damage a relationship that didn't need to be damaged
There's no real risk — treating every case as deliberate is always the safest approach
The risk is purely legal, not interpersonal
This failure mode only applies to relationships with direct managers, not peers
items.explanation: L2 explicitly warns that over-interpreting a single ambiguous incident risks unnecessary relationship damage — the risk is interpersonal, not purely legal.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's wrong with responding to black politics with black politics (e.g., retaliating with a rumor of your own)?
choices: It trades one form of trust damage for another and rarely improves the underlying situation
It's actually the most effective response and is recommended by L2
It's wrong only because it's against most companies' written policies
There's no real downside as long as the retaliation is proportionate
items.explanation: L2 explicitly frames retaliation-in-kind as trading one form of damage for another, not as an effective or recommended countermeasure.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does the colleague's exact wording ("the approach I came up with") matter in the Scenario?
choices: It's a stronger, more specific claim of direct authorship than a passive omission, making it harder to explain as purely accidental
The exact wording is irrelevant — only the outcome (no credit given) matters
The wording matters only because it was said in a formal written document, not spoken aloud
The wording is irrelevant because leadership never reacts to specific phrasing
items.explanation: L3 specifically distinguishes an active authorship claim from a passive omission — the former is harder to explain away as accidental.

items.prompt: Per L3, what makes a second or third instance of the same behavior different from the first, evidentially?
choices: The pattern itself becomes the evidence — no single incident needs to be airtight if multiple incidents point the same direction
A second instance is always legally actionable while a first instance never is
Nothing changes — each instance must be evaluated in complete isolation from the others
A second instance automatically means the first instance should be disregarded entirely
items.explanation: L3 explicitly treats a repeated pattern as cumulative evidence, reducing the need for any single incident to be independently airtight.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does the engineer's in-meeting response avoid directly accusing the colleague?
choices: A public correction or confrontation in front of leadership often reads as an interpersonal conflict, which can reflect worse on the person raising it regardless of who's right
Direct accusations are illegal to make in a professional meeting setting
The engineer isn't confident enough in their own work to make any claim at all
Company policy universally forbids ever mentioning who did what work
items.explanation: L3 frames the low-confrontation approach as a calibrated risk management move, not a legal requirement or a lack of confidence.

items.prompt: What does the engineer's actual in-meeting line accomplish, per L3?
choices: It factually places the engineer's name next to the work in the room, without accusing anyone, correcting the record for attentive listeners
It publicly and directly accuses the colleague of stealing credit in front of leadership
It changes the subject entirely away from the pricing analysis
It formally requests that HR investigate the colleague's conduct
items.explanation: L3 describes the line as a low-risk, non-accusatory way to correct the record — not a public accusation, topic change, or HR request.

items.prompt: Per L3, does the calm in-meeting correction fully resolve whether this was a one-time lapse or part of a pattern?
choices: No — it corrects the immediate record but doesn't address the underlying question, which the private follow-up conversation is meant to explore
Yes — the in-meeting correction is described as a complete and final resolution
No, because the in-meeting correction actually makes the situation worse
Yes, but only if the colleague apologizes on the spot
items.explanation: L3 explicitly separates the two purposes: the in-meeting move corrects the record, while the private conversation addresses the pattern question.

items.prompt: Per L3, what's the value of asking the colleague about it privately ("can you help me understand what happened") instead of assuming the worst?
choices: It gives the colleague a real chance to explain, and if the same thing happens again afterward, that repeat is much stronger evidence of intent than the first incident alone
It guarantees the colleague will admit wrongdoing immediately
It has no real value — the outcome would be identical either way
It's valuable only because it creates a legal record admissible in court
items.explanation: L3 frames the private question as both fair (a genuine chance to explain) and strategically useful (sharpening the evidentiary value of any repeat).

items.prompt: Per L3's "what generalizes" section, does the core lesson about calibrating response to evidence strength apply only to credit-stealing?
choices: No — it generalizes to the other four black-politics tactics from L2's table, not just credit-stealing
Yes — the lesson is stated to apply exclusively to credit-stealing and no other tactic
No, but only to tactics that happen in front of leadership specifically
Yes, but only within engineering teams specifically
items.explanation: L3 explicitly extends the core lesson (calibrating response to whether it's one incident or a pattern) beyond credit-stealing to the other tactics.

items.prompt: Per L3, would the exact in-meeting line ("happy to walk through the assumptions, since I built that model") work equally well for responding to scapegoating?
choices: No — that specific move only works for credit-stealing, where the fix is re-attaching a name to existing work; scapegoating needs a differently-shaped response
Yes — the exact same line works identically for any black-politics tactic
Yes, but only if the word "model" is replaced with "decision"
No, because that line only works in written communication, never spoken aloud
items.explanation: L3 explicitly notes the specific move is shaped for credit-stealing's particular mechanism and doesn't transfer directly to a tactic like scapegoating.
